title: Lesson 12: Change Management as a Deliverable, Not an Afterthought
description: Treating each meaningful change to a live delivery as its own bounded deliverable with a scope, a named risk, a test, a rollback, and a record, instead of a drive-by edit that quietly erodes a working system.

questions.question: Why is a drive-by change to a live delivery a problem?
options: It is usually much larger than it looks and tends to break the whole build outright
Something now depends on the current behavior, and the change goes unrecorded
It costs considerably more compute to apply than a planned change would
It requires the client's legal team to review and sign a new agreement
questions.explanation: After handover the client's week is built around the current behavior, so a small unrecorded edit alters someone else's operation. A stream of them leaves nobody able to say what the system does.

questions.question: What should be written before a change lands?
options: The rollback plan, specific to the exact prior state
The follow-up change that will improve on it later
The announcement telling the client it already shipped
The estimate of the hours the change consumed
questions.explanation: A change that cannot be reverted cleanly is one you cannot afford to be wrong about. The revert, tied to the precise prior configuration, is written before the change, not improvised after.

questions.question: A change to a job that runs unattended needs what?
options: No gate at all, since no person is present to notice a failure
A gate or check that runs after the change, because no person is watching
A larger scope that bundles in any other tidy-ups while you are already there
A blanket approval mode shared with interactive, human-driven work
questions.explanation: When nothing human is in the loop, the only thing that notices a bad change is an automated guard or eval. What separates a safe change from a dangerous one is often whether anything is watching after it lands.
